CHAPTER IV. Agriculture and Forests. The tea industry has exhibited a marked develop- Tea inf¬ luent in this district during the last decade. The area try< under tea has increased from 40,497 to 44,177 acres, and the total outturn of manufactured tea by about 70 per cent. Nearly all the available land to the north of the Trunk Road between the Belsirl river and the Sapoi road has been taken up and cleared for tea cultivation. Further west, in the Borchola and Orang mauzas, there have recently been numerous applications for special leases for land suitable for tea, and there can be little doubt that if the prospects of the industry continue good, a large proportion of the stretches of waste land in this part of the district will soon be brought under cultivation. The area under jute also shows a marked tendency Jute, to increase. The yield last year (1913-14) was about 100,000 maunds. This crop is cultivated largely by Nepalis who have settled in the district, particularly in the Behali circle. Since 1905 the only addition to the reserved forests ^served has been a small area of 40 acres which was added to forests, the Gamiri reserve in 1913. Proposals for an addition 2 to the Charduar reserve, and also for the formation of a new reserve in the north-east of the district and of game reserves in Gohpur and Orang mauzas are now under the consideration of Government. CHAPTER VI. Economic condition of thb people. Wag** and As in other districts in the province prices of rice and prices. other food stuffs have shown- a steady tendency to increase during the past ten years. This has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in the rate of wages of the labouring classes. The average daily wage of a day labourer is now eight annas as compared with

five or six annas some ten years ago. At the same time the question of an adequate supply of labour is becoming one of increasing difficulty each year. Commnnica. During the last three or four years there has been a ‘ions. marked improvement in communications throughout the district. This is largely due to the generous special grants recently given by Government for the purpose. In the sadr subdivision a new road has been constructed linking the Balipara road with the Sootia-Coldarghat road and having a ferry crossing at the Bliarali. This road connects the Tezpur and Bishnatli tea districts. Portions of the Gharali-Biswanath, the Belsiri-Balipara and the North Trunk roads have been much improved by metalling. In the north of the Mangaldai subdivision new roads have been constructed, connecting the stations on the Rangiya-Tangla extension of the Eastern Bengal State Railway with the tea gardens. The revenue demand of the district has considerably Lai increased during the past 10 years. The settled a’ •' in T iue ' 1906-06 was 435,422 acres with a revenue d d of Rs. 7,39,400. The area in 1913-14 had rioen to 613,656 acres with a revenue demand of Its. 8,60,076, showing an increase of 78,134 acres in area and of Rs. 1,20,676 in revenue. The rate of expansion has been continuously maintained except in 1909-10 when there was a fall of Rs. 6,074 in the revenue demand as compared with the previous year. The decrease was more apparent than real, as the preparation of correct statistics in that year was complicated by the resettle¬ ment operations. The gradual increase is attributed to the expansion of ordinary cultivation brought about chiefly by Nepali settlers, ear-garden coolies, and settlers from Mymensingh who have occupied the riverain mauzas in the south of Mangaldai, princi¬ pally in connection with the cultivation of jute. 4 Excise. The principal exoiseable article of consumption in this district is opium, accounting, as it does, for nearly three-fourths of the excise revenue. The consumption

was highest in 1908-09 when it amounted to 222 maunds. In the following two years there was a con¬ siderable drop, but last year (1913-14) it rose again to 210 maunds. The habit is most widespread in the Mangaldai subdivision, where nearly all the Kacharia and lower class Assamese are addicted to it. The habit of smoking the drug is said to be on the increase, and it is estimated that not less than half the consumers are smokers. In order to restrict the use of the drug the treasury price has been gradually raised from Its. 37 to Hs. 42 per seer, and the number of retail shops reduced from 98 in 1905-06 to 54 in 1912-13. The outstill system was discontinued in 1908-09 and since then the contract distillery system has been in force. The spirit is manufactured at Jorhat and is sent down to the Tezpur warehouse where it is reduced to strengths of 30 IT. P. and 60 U. P. and issued to the retail vendors. Though the population has increased, consumption has remained nearly stationary and it is generally agreed that drunkenness is decreasing. Government sanctioned in 1912 the establishment of a new outpost at Dhekiajuli within the jurisdiction of Tezpur police station. This was necessary for the convenience of neighbouring villages and also on account of the new tea areas in Borohola mauza. The outpost has not been opened yet, but the buildings are under construction. This dread disease appears to be gradually dying out in the district, though it is still fairly widespread in the Mangaldai subdivision. The number of deaths attributed to it decreased from 1,106 in 1905 to 399 in 3913, The following is quoted from the report of the All-India Sanitary Conference of 1912-13 on kala-azar. “ Tezpur subdivision .—There are only two villages which are certainly infected and 14 which contain one or two very doubtful cases. The infection has practically died out of the Tezpur subdivision. 5 “ Past hiitary.—No record is traoeable exoept the fact thatjhere was some mortality from kala-azar in 1896. “ In {Daogaon Pukri which is one of the two undoubtedly infected villages the people state that

during the epidemic of kala-azar the viotims died almost as suddenly as in a cholera epidemic. “ The general opinion in the district is that iala- azar has almost disappeared. This is also the opinion of the Conference. " It appears that propagation of kola-azar is in this way: An area gets infected by importation. The infection spreads and a panio is established. Infected families who have lost one or two of their numbers and see others dying decide to migrate elsewhere to an uninfected area. They do so, if uncheoked, taking with them an infected person or the seeds of the disease. This leads to the propagation of the disease in this area and the process then repeats itself.” As in other districts in the province, the cause of Education, education shows steady and satisfactory progress. CHAPTER IV. Agriculture and Forests. The tea industry has exhibited a marked develop- Tea inf¬ luent in this district during the last decade. The area try< under tea has increased from 40,497 to 44,177 acres, and the total outturn of manufactured tea by about 70 per cent. Nearly all the available land to the north of the Trunk Road between the Belsirl river and the Sapoi road has been taken up and cleared for tea cultivation. Further west, in the Borchola and Orang mauzas, there have recently been numerous applications for special leases for land suitable for tea, and there can be little doubt that if the prospects of the industry continue good, a large proportion of the stretches of waste land in this part of the district will soon be brought under cultivation. The area under jute also shows a marked tendency Jute, to increase. The yield last year (1913-14) was about 100,000 maunds. This crop is cultivated largely by Nepalis who have settled in the district, particularly in the Behali circle. Since 1905 the only addition to the reserved forests ^served has been a small area of 40 acres which was added to forests, the Gamiri reserve in 1913. Proposals for an addition 2 to the Charduar reserve, and also for the formation of a new reserve in the north-east of the district and of game reserves in Gohpur and Orang mauzas are now under the consideration of Government. CHAPTER VI. Economic condition of thb people. Wag** and As in other districts in the province prices of rice and prices. other food stuffs have shown- a steady tendency to increase during the past ten years. This has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in the rate of wages of the labouring classes. The average daily wage of a day labourer is now eight annas as compared with

five or six annas some ten years ago. At the same time the question of an adequate supply of labour is becoming one of increasing difficulty each year. Commnnica. During the last three or four years there has been a ‘ions. marked improvement in communications throughout the district. This is largely due to the generous special grants recently given by Government for the purpose. In the sadr subdivision a new road has been constructed linking the Balipara road with the Sootia-Coldarghat road and having a ferry crossing at the Bliarali. This road connects the Tezpur and Bishnatli tea districts. Portions of the Gharali-Biswanath, the Belsiri-Balipara and the North Trunk roads have been much improved by metalling. In the north of the Mangaldai subdivision new roads have been constructed, connecting the stations on the Rangiya-Tangla extension of the Eastern Bengal State Railway with the tea gardens. The rate of expansion has been continuously maintained except in 1909-10 when there was a fall of Rs. 6,074 in the revenue demand as compared with the previous year. The decrease was more apparent than real, as the preparation of correct statistics in that year was complicated by the resettle¬ ment operations. The gradual increase is attributed to the expansion of ordinary cultivation brought about chiefly by Nepali settlers, ear-garden coolies, and settlers from Mymensingh who have occupied the riverain mauzas in the south of Mangaldai, princi¬ pally in connection with the cultivation of jute. 4 Excise. The principal exoiseable article of consumption in this district is opium, accounting, as it does, for nearly three-fourths of the excise revenue. The consumption

was highest in 1908-09 when it amounted to 222 maunds. In the following two years there was a con¬ siderable drop, but last year (1913-14) it rose again to 210 maunds. The habit is most widespread in the Mangaldai subdivision, where nearly all the Kacharia and lower class Assamese are addicted to it. The habit of smoking the drug is said to be on the increase, and it is estimated that not less than half the consumers are smokers. In order to restrict the use of the drug the treasury price has been gradually raised from Its. 37 to Hs. 42 per seer, and the number of retail shops reduced from 98 in 1905-06 to 54 in 1912-13. The outstill system was discontinued in 1908-09 and since then the contract distillery system has been in force. The spirit is manufactured at Jorhat and is sent down to the Tezpur warehouse where it is reduced to strengths of 30 IT. P. and 60 U. P. and issued to the retail vendors. Though the population has increased, consumption has remained nearly stationary and it is generally agreed that drunkenness is decreasing. Government sanctioned in 1912 the establishment of a new outpost at Dhekiajuli within the jurisdiction of Tezpur police station. This was necessary for the convenience of neighbouring villages and also on account of the new tea areas in Borohola mauza. The outpost has not been opened yet, but the buildings are under construction. Infected families who have lost one or two of their numbers and see others dying decide to migrate elsewhere to an uninfected area. They do so, if uncheoked, taking with them an infected person or the seeds of the disease.
